They produce electricity and heat as long as fuel is supplied. A fuel cell consists of two electrodes—a negative electrode (or anode) and a positive electrode (or cathode)—sandwiched around an electrolyte. A fuel, such as hydrogen, is fed to the anode, and air is fed to the cathode. In a polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cell, a catalyst separates hydrogen atoms into protons and electrons, which take different paths to the cathode. The electrons go through an external circuit, creating a flow of electricity. Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells produce electricity through a chemical reaction between hydrogen and oxygen. In a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen and oxygen are used as fuel. The process begins with the introduction of hydrogen on the anode side and oxygen on the cathode side. The hydrogen molecules (H2) are split into two protons (H+) and two electrons (e-) at the anode. This process is facilitated by a catalyst, typically made of platinum. The protons then pass through a proton exchange membrane (PEM), which only allows protons to pass through and blocks the electrons. This forces the electrons to travel through an external circuit, creating an electric current. This is the electricity that the fuel cell produces. On the cathode side, oxygen molecules (O2) are introduced. The oxygen molecules react with the protons that have passed through the PEM and the electrons that have travelled through the external circuit to form water (H2O). This reaction also releases heat, which can be used for additional power. The overall reaction in a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell is 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O + heat + electricity. This
